analysis.one_liner: Lets banks opt out of Sarbanes-Oxley executive certifications and internal control audits.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the 2002 Sarbanes-Oxley law, which was passed after the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals. It would have required the Securities and Exchange Commission to let insured banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies choose not to have their top executives personally certify their financial reports and not to prepare the internal-control reports required by Sarbanes-Oxley. Those rules exist so investors can trust that a company's financial statements are accurate and that someone accountable signs off on them. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Executives and shareholders of publicly traded banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies. They would save the compliance cost of executive certifications and internal-control reporting, and executives would no longer personally sign off on the accuracy of their companies' financial reports [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Executives and shareholders of public banks

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require SEC rules to let insured depository institutions, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies voluntarily skip the executive certification of quarterly and annual reports required by Sarbanes-Oxley Section 302 [S2][S3].

It would also let those same financial firms skip the management assessment of internal controls required by Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404, which is designed to catch weak or fraudulent financial controls [S2][S3].
Because the opt-out is voluntary, each covered firm could decide case by case whether the reduced compliance burden outweighs the loss of investor confidence from dropping the certifications [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors in publicly traded banks. Without executive certifications and internal-control reports, they would have weaker assurance that the financial statements and controls of a bank they own are sound, the very assurance Sarbanes-Oxley created after accounting scandals wiped out shareholders [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Removing Section 302 and Section 404 obligations for banks would reduce the transparency and accountability Congress imposed after corporate accounting scandals, leaving shareholders with less reliable information about the firms they own [S2][S3].

A bank that opts out could signal weaker internal controls to investors and regulators, potentially raising its cost of capital; the bill offers no safeguard tying the exemption to a firm's safety and soundness [S3].

The bill arrived in March 2008, as the financial system was coming under severe strain, which made loosening financial reporting rules a hard argument to win; opponents would say this was the wrong time to reduce oversight of financial institutions [S1][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: banks save compliance costs on certifications and internal-control reporting, and some small community banks have long argued Sarbanes-Oxley costs them disproportionate sums. The cost falls on a broader group: investors in public banks lose the personal accountability of executives certifying financial statements, and the financial system loses a layer of control reporting at a moment, in 2008, when confidence in financial institutions was the scarce resource. On balance the bill traded a broad, systemic safeguard for a concentrated, private saving.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Dole introduced the bill on March 5, 2008, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
The bill's entire action history consists of its introduction and committee referral; no further action was taken during the 110th Congress [S5].
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2009, and the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public investors in banks are better off, since the executive certifications and internal-control reporting requirements remain in force. Bank executives who would have saved compliance costs gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bank investors; the reporting rules stayed

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Dole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies from Sarbanes-Oxley Sections 302 and 404 [S1][S3].

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 5, 2008 and took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsor was a Republican with a single Democratic cosponsor [S1][S4].

industries.industry: Publicly traded banks, bank holding companies, and savings-and-loan holding companies
industries.note: The bill would let them opt out of Sarbanes-Oxley executive certifications and internal-control reports, saving compliance costs while reducing the information and accountability available to their shareholders [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Audit and accounting firms serving financial institutions
industries.note: Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 generates paid audit work on internal controls; firms that opted out would no longer need that assurance work [S3].
